knowledgelake
Case study · Data engineering · Python

110 messy files in,
one clean knowledge base out

knowledgelake turns a pile of technical documents (text PDFs, scanned PDFs, saved LinkedIn carousels, question-only lists) into a de-duplicated, searchable knowledge base that grows every time new documents land.

The problem

Same questions everywhere, answers nowhere

Technical material piles up fast. "Second highest salary" appeared in four different files. "Explain medallion architecture" appeared in six. Some lists had questions with no answers at all, and half the best content was trapped in images. Nobody can read all of that every time they need an answer, so I built a pipeline to do the sorting.

Pipeline

Seven stages, one command, two review queues

# first run, then every time new notes arrive kb ingest notes.zip --kb kb_store --build # → {"files": 110, "questions_found": 2022, "added": ..., "already_in_kb": ...}
Engineering decisions

The parts that took thinking

De-duplication

Similar is not the same

Token overlap alone would merge questions that mean opposite things. Before merging, the pipeline requires both questions to share the same meaning-critical words (numbers, highest/lowest, before/after, never, left/right).

merge · "Find the 2nd highest salary" ≈ "Retrieve second-highest salary"keep apart · "…second highest salary" vs "…second lowest salary"
Scale

Near-linear candidate search

Comparing every pair of 2,022 questions means about 2 million comparisons. An inverted index (token → question ids) generates only plausible pairs, then union-find groups the duplicate chains in one pass.

Classification

Context from the source file

"How do you do an incremental load?" could be ADF, Databricks or SQL. A second pass gives each question a small bonus toward its file's dominant topic. Measured against my 1,775 hand-labelled items, keyword rules reach 83.4% topic accuracy.

Incremental loads

Appending is idempotent

New batches are checked against the stored questions, not just against each other. Re-ingesting the same zip adds 0 and only records the extra source. The same watermark-style thinking I use in production pipelines.

Version 2

Measured upgrades, not just more features

For v2 I turned my own manual review from v1 into labelled data: every pair I merged or rejected by hand. Replaying those decisions reproduces the curated 1,775 exactly, so every upgrade below is scored against real ground truth.

Record linkage

Duplicates as entity resolution

Plain embedding similarity did worse than word overlap, because SQL questions that differ in one word look alike. So I used blocking (k-nearest neighbours), pair scoring (a logistic-regression model on 11 features, including answer similarity) and a review queue. To find 70% of the duplicates you check 1,407 pairs instead of 36,382.

Classification

Rules plus a model that knows when it's unsure

A model trained on the knowledge base itself, blended with the keyword rules: 85.2% under leave-source-file-out cross-validation. More useful is its confidence score. Review the least confident 20% and the other 80% are 93.7% correct.

Data quality

A scale test found two real bugs

Re-feeding all 110 files into the finished KB should add nothing. It added 922. Common words were being dropped from the similarity score, and "What is PySpark?" had no tokens left to compare. After the fixes, a second re-ingest adds 0.

GenAI

Ask my notes

Hybrid retrieval (keyword + embeddings, fused with reciprocal rank fusion) feeds Claude, which answers only from the notes and cites them. On 234 real paraphrased questions: Recall@5 73.5% vs 65.0% keyword-only.

What I'd do next

Honest limits

  • Topic accuracy is capped by overlapping topics (ADF vs. Azure platform vs. general concepts), where even my own labels are debatable. Multi-label topics would fit better than a harder classifier.
  • Paraphrase duplicates still need a human to confirm. The model ranks the review queue well, but auto-merging paraphrases at useful recall costs too much precision.
  • My build environment couldn't download pretrained models, so the measured embeddings are TF-IDF + LSA trained on my notes. The sentence-transformers backend is wired in but not yet measured.
  • Most remaining noise comes from the parser on OCR'd infographic carousels. That's the next thing to fix.
